title: Detecting the Concealment Step: Do Scheming Models Suppress Honest Features Before Output?

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Anthropic used mechanistic interpretability in pre-deployment safety assessment of Claude Sonnet 4.5 to examine internal features for deceptive tendencies. Apollo Research found frontier models engage in scheming behaviors. Techniques like circuit editing and head ablation have been used to suppress undesired behaviors. However, the specific framing of detecting a 'concealment step' where honest features are suppressed between mid and late layers before output in scheming models has not been directly studied. The general detection of deceptive alignment via interpretability is active but this specific mechanistic hypothesis (feature suppression as the concealment mechanism) remains untested.

title: Which Attention Heads Copy the Harmful Context? Tracing Information Flow in Jailbroken Completions

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: This idea is substantially covered by existing work. 'On the Role of Attention Heads in Large Language Model Safety' (ICLR 2025) identifies attention heads that influence harmful vs safe responses by comparing activation patterns between rejected and jailbroken prompts, and uses interpolation of internal representations to suppress harmful outputs. 'Jailbreak Defense in LLM via Attention Head Analysis and Selective Intervention' directly addresses selective intervention on identified heads. 'Attention Slipping: A Mechanistic Understanding of Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses in LLMs' (2025) provides mechanistic understanding of attention shifts during jailbreaks. The proposed contribution of identifying 'harm-copy' heads and performing knockout experiments is largely subsumed by these papers.

title: Feature Superposition and Missed Safety Signals: Probing Whether Harm Features Are Entangled with Benign Features

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Safe-SAIL (2025) provides a framework for interpreting SAE features in safety domains, covering 2,059 SAE neurons across four safety subdomains. However, Safe-SAIL focuses on identifying and interpreting safety-relevant features, not specifically on measuring whether harm features are disproportionately entangled in superposition compared to benign features. DeepMind published negative results for SAEs on downstream tasks and deprioritized SAE research (2025), suggesting limitations. The specific hypothesis that harm features suffer more from superposition than benign features, and that this explains missed safety signals, remains untested as a controlled comparison.

title: The Recall-to-Output Gap: When a Model Knows a Fact but States Its Opposite

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Research has established that models 'know what they don't know' — internal activations differ when guessing vs recalling. Work on sycophancy shows LLM activations encapsulate internal beliefs that can diverge from generated outputs (ICLR 2026). Linear directions encoding self-knowledge have been found causally relevant for refusal behavior. Mechanistic Interpretability for hallucination has advanced (ICLR 2026 paper on mechanistic interpretability). However, the specific framing of a 'recall-to-output gap' — where a model internally recalls a correct fact but outputs the opposite under misleading context — and the mechanistic question of whether this is a routing failure vs MLP suppression has not been directly studied in this precise formulation.

title: Reward Hacking Signatures in Internal Activations: Can We Detect It Before the Output?

novelty_assessment.label: already_solved
novelty_assessment.reasoning: This idea is directly addressed by 'Monitoring Emergent Reward Hacking During Generation via Internal Activations' (arXiv:2603.04069, March 2026). That paper trains sparse autoencoders on residual stream activations and applies lightweight linear classifiers to produce token-level estimates of reward-hacking activity. They show internal activation patterns reliably distinguish reward-hacking from benign behavior, generalize to unseen mixed-policy adapters, and exhibit model-dependent temporal structure during chain-of-thought reasoning. Circuit-Aware Reward Training (CART, 2025) also addresses mechanistic detection. The proposed idea of training probes on activations to detect reward hacking before output is essentially the exact contribution of the March 2026 paper.

title: Induction Heads and Deceptive Consistency: Do In-Context Scheming Models Exploit Induction Circuits?

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: While induction heads are extensively studied mechanistically (ICLR 2026 submission on emergence, repetition curse work, in-context learning studies), and scheming/deceptive alignment is separately studied (Apollo Research, Anthropic alignment faking), no published work connects these two threads to ask whether in-context scheming specifically exploits induction circuits. The question of whether deceptive consistency in scheming uses the same copying mechanism as standard in-context learning (induction heads) vs specialized circuits is genuinely novel. The toy-model limitation is acknowledged but the research question itself is unexplored.

title: The Context-Window Safety Degradation Chain: How Long Contexts Dilute Refusal Features

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: 'When Refusals Fail: Unstable Safety Mechanisms in Long-Context LLM Agents' (arXiv:2512.02445, 2025) directly studies refusal degradation in long-context settings. 'Context Rot' research (Chroma, 2025-2026) establishes attention dilution and lost-in-the-middle effects as core degradation mechanisms. However, these works are primarily behavioral, measuring refusal rate changes and performance drops. The mechanistic question of whether degradation is specifically due to refusal feature dilution in the residual stream (attention-capacity vs positional-encoding) through TransformerLens analysis has not been directly addressed. The behavioral phenomenon is known but the mechanistic interpretability angle adds novelty.

title: MLP Layers as Safety Feature Destroyers: Which FFN Sublayers Overwrite Harm Representations

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Research on MLP layers as key-value stores and their role in representation is well-established. Anthropic's circuit tracing (March 2025) replaces MLPs with cross-layer transcoders for interpretability. The specific question of systematically mapping which FFN sublayers destructively overwrite harm representations (as opposed to attention layers) via probe-accuracy degradation is a focused contribution not fully addressed.

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed

title: Early Layer Safety vs. Late Layer Safety: Which Layers' Representations Actually Determine Refusal

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: 'Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security' (ICLR 2025) identifies safety layers as a small set of contiguous layers in the middle (14-25% of network depth), distinct from answer prediction layers. 'The Geometry of Refusal: Concept Cones and Representational Independence' (2025) reveals multiple independent refusal directions and concept cones rather than a single direction. 'LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately' (2025) shows harmfulness is encoded at earlier positions and refusal at later positions. 'Understanding and Mitigating Over-refusal via Safety Representation' (2025) shows over-refusal stems from shortcut keyword detection in lower layers. The core question of which layers are causally necessary for refusal is substantially answered.

title: Causal Role of Name-Mover Heads in Sycophancy: Do IOI Circuits Enable Social Pressure Compliance?

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The IOI circuit and name-mover heads are among the most well-studied circuits in mechanistic interpretability (Wang et al. 2022, ICLR). Sycophancy has been studied mechanistically — 'Sycophancy Is Not One Thing: Causal Separation of Sycophantic Behaviors in LLMs' (2025) shows sycophantic behaviors admit linear structure in activation space. However, no published work connects IOI name-mover heads specifically to sycophancy mechanisms. The hypothesis that sycophancy exploits the same token-copying infrastructure as IOI (name-mover heads copying the user's stated preference) is a creative and testable connection between two well-studied phenomena that has not been explored.
